posts.name: HeroComplex
posts.cooked:
Syntactic Analysis actually doesn't work for Critical Multiplier anyway---the cards have just been revealed, which means they are still in the deck.  Since Critical Multiplier only triggers on discards from your hand, discarding the revealed cards from your deck doesn't help.  Quick Calculation wouldn't interact with Critical Multiplier, either, even if it discarded from deck rather than put them on the bottom.  I think the only cards Parse has that allow her to discard are Segmentation Fault, Snap Decision, and Recompile, for a total of 7, but I may be overlooking one.

For those discard-from-deck cards to work with Critical Multiplier, they'd have to come up with a different kind of wording, something like "draw and immediately discard."  In some competitive card games, that'd be a problem, since your hand is not public and cards can essentially vanish into it.  But I imagine it would work in Sentinels if that's a functionality they ever wanted.

After several plays with Parse, I've managed to convince myself of a useful lesson—it is okay to discard cards that you actually want.  The first few games, I was seeing the potential uses of all of her cards, so I didn't want to discard any of them to Recompile, because then I wouldn't have them.  So I was avoiding using Recompile because it was going to be a discard of the 1 card I was okay losing to draw just 2, which was not really impressive, and even if I had out a Critical Multiplier wouldn't do much.  But now that I've gotten more used to her, including the frequency of cards in her deck and how much she's able to draw/discard, I've realized that it's okay to chuck good cards.  While I might want to keep that copy of Gauge around just in case I want to start using it, if I'm going full-throttle on Recompile I've got a decent chance of just drawing a second copy, in addition to a bunch of other cards that add to my options.  While I certainly like her cards, and they're generally speaking all at least useful enough to play and genuinely benefit from, most are not so critical to Parse's gameplay that you need to jealously guard them in your hand because if you discard one you've thrown away your whole strategy or shot yourself in the foot.  She has various control cards that provide backup coverage, in case you only have one or the other, and she has various different ways to contribute damage, with varying levels of utility depending on the matchup, so even if you pitch one you'll probably find another that can add similar utility.

Being willing to give up that control over every single card in my hand let me do a lot more with her.  Now I'm filling up my hand much easier with Recompile—which, if I have out Critical Multiplier, can potentially help out other heroes at the same time that it helps me, as a nice bonus.  Discarding 3 to draw 6 is an impressive effect already, so the fact that it can also contribute 3 (or more) damage is a solid bonus from the card interaction.  Yeah, that took two card plays, but Critical Multiplier will keep working over the course of the game—if you Recompile once, it's already contributing as much damage as a 3-point one-shot would have, but often with more versatility because you can spread it out among heroes or bunch it up depending on the board.  If later that turn you use Segmentation Fault, it's up to 4 damage from just that turn, in addition to the actual effects you got from your play and power.  By the end of the game, Critical Multiplier can give you far more damage than almost any single one-shot would, for doing stuff that you'd do anyway.  So, yes, it's an extra play in addition to the Recompile, etc., but that's exactly how it should be.

Critical Multiplier reminds me of playing Chrono-Ranger.  Just a 1-damage plink is not that impressive, but the fact that you get them from all over the place, from playing cards that you'd want to play anyway, lets you really start to take advantage of them.  And playing a Bounty may not by itself feel useful, but then on your next play, you get increased value from whatever you were going to do anyway.  Playing that Bounty meant that you didn't get to play an "active" card on your previous turn, so you need to learn when a Bounty is the right play and when it's not, but over the course of several turns, you can get a ton of damage from it, just by continuing to play your cards normally.  Yes, it's from two card plays, and when first playing a deck like Parse's or Chrono-Ranger's, I imagine it's common to see that as an inconvenience, but once you get used to playing the deck, those interactions instead start to shine as synergy.

posts.cooked:
Ameena:

Plinky death with lots of irreducible damage. And the ability to let other people do irreducible damage (off the top of my head, I'm not sure who else can do that besides Mr Fixer and GI Bunker).

Plinks don't do incredibly much good against a villain with 80 or 100 HP, not unless you can boost them or just have a never-ending supply (or, like Chrono-Ranger, both).  Parse's damage output looks almost comparable to Haka's, but he has way more HP and better card draw.  And as I've often said, irreducible only matters against villains who have reduction, and significant reduction is present on maybe a third of villains and a couple environments.  Entire cards that exist only to grant irreducibility are usually wasted cards; irreducible on something that does other things and just happens to be irreducible is very nice, but seldom all-deciding.  I've yet to see a card that deals 20 irreducible damage; you can't really win the game with just 3 points here and 1 point there, whether it's reducible or not.

And the ability to, as mentioned, build up some epic damage via Critical Multiplier(s), especially if you have Recompile and at least three other cards.

We seem to have different definitions of epic.  Critical Multiplier can be counted on for an average of +1 damage per copy of the card, if you have some effect that will let you discard (a handful of villains and environs will help you with discarding, but you can't really count on it).  Guise + CM is a nice combo if you can manage it, but only nets +1 per turn; handy but not sexy.  Recompile is just a one-shot, and if used to absolute maximum effect, it could offer +27 to a single damage instance - not quite enough to one-shot Iron Legacy unless the recipient is Ra or Tempest, and certainly barely enough for Citizen Dawn or Omnitron to even notice, and entirely wasted against the individual small targets that you're often busy dealing with.  Considering how much work you have to go to setting it up (drawing and playing all three copies of CM, needing a discard besides that, and praying not to get wiped), the reward should be pretty close to an instant win - at least something akin to End of Days, which is just one card, and a lot of heroes have a single card almost that potent.  The only one I've seen for Parse that looks able to clinch victories like that is the Iron Legacy one whose name I keep forgetting - I actually did get that one in play after reading about it in this guide, but naturally I was against the Vengeance Five at the time, so it wasn't that hot.  Against a normal villain, though, it's great - possibly a Dark Visionary level of great, in which case the problem would stop being "useless" and start becoming "broken and unfun".  But only if you happen to draw it.

What I am definitely not getting from Parse is consistency.  She does a little of this, a little of that, and almost never enough of anything to be crucial to victory.

Were there characters you didn't like before Vengeance came along?

I'd say Expatriette tops the list, closely followed by Bunker, Fixer, and eventually Haka (who is good, just not as good as I'd like).  Oh, and Legacy; he's awesome and great at winning games, but I don't enjoy playing him at all (though Young Legacy was okay).  I like Wraith every once in a while, she's got a lot of neat options, but too often she falls into a predictable pattern and becomes boring fast.  Ra has a similar problem and is less entertaining, though I love the Egyptian theme; he's too simple to entirely do it for me, though certainly good to have on your team.  Visionary has neat things she can do, but wastes too many cards on piddly plinks of psychic damage, and largely sidelines the reality-warping awesomeness she's mostly about to me.  Tachyon is just barely on the verge of beginning to bore me.  Did I forget anyone?  I think pretty much everyone that's left qualifies as awesomesauce to me…oh, except maybe for Setback, who I haven't really started to grok, and who seems kinda all over the place, but I don't really feel like I've figured him out yet beyond "he's pretty tanky and does a bit of melee damage".  Parse, I do feel like I know what she can do, I'm just not very satisfied with the result as yet.

but for example did you think that Unity was bad because sometimes she can't do anything (mainly when she has equipment but no bots, or vice-versa)?

She can have that problem, but in my experience skipping your turn to draw 2 once is usually sufficient to get her out of that scrape.  I've had one or two bad games as her, but never enough to sour me on the experience.  Probably in large part this is due to me really liking her personality and cute visuals.  Parse is a neat character too, but doesn't quite turn it up to 11 the same way.

I tend to find that I like each wave of new heroes more than previous ones. That's not to say that I dislike any of the older heroes (I don't dislike any of them), but I find I have more favourites from the later expansions (well, from Infernal Relics onwards) than from the older stuff.

The same is true here, but I think that has more to do with the heroes themselves.  It's likely that the >G crew's understanding of design technology has progressed, but mostly I think they just waited until the game was well-proven before they got really experimental with what the heroes could do.  Both IR heroes are Complexity 3s, and both are extremely high on the awesomeness scale; since then, there really haven't been any simplistic heroes like Ra or Legs or Haka.  Even complexity-1 KNYFE gives you tons and tons of stuff to do, and took two games for me to begin understanding her.  It makes sense for the core-set heroes to be more straightforward (even AZ, while counterintuitive and mathy to play, isn't as complex a Complexity-3 as the other two), since they're responsible for selling the game to newbies; Rook City was probably just an early design and not too adventurous.  Since then, they're really going above and beyond, so unsurprisingly the results are quite good.  Parse might prove to be the same thing in time, but so far she feels to me more like a failed experiment.

As well as playing more games in general, it may help to play more games with other people - I think I recall you saying you solo quite a lot. It can help to play with different people, because then you get to see how they play each hero, and that might show you new ways of playing them which you'd never thought of before.

Well, unfortunately, that's a problem that's slow to solve itself.  If I'm lucky I can get in two non-solo games in a week.

~ 3 points here and one point there is no good

Try telling that to the Hired Gun/Thief/Informant/Voss's Minions etc…and expand that list if Parse has even a +1 damage buff from anywhere.

~Critical Multiplier is no good because reasons.

Parse has plenty of ways of discarding stuff - Recompile just happens to be her personal best. Plenty of villains and environments force discards as well. Also, with the max discard from Recompile you get back six cards. Six! Can anyone else draw that many at once? The only person I can think of who can manage it would be Fanatic when her only available card is Prayer of Desparation. Drawing that many cards, you are bound to get something useful, even if it isn't a copy of Critical Multiplier. Get all three copies of it out (I've managed two on more than one occasion…think I've only managed all three once but I've not played Parse too many times) and you can give a total of +3 damage to whomever you like just for discarding one card. Now say you're fighting Voss, who has several Minions out, and have built up a nice stack of damage on…well, anyone, really, as long as they haven't dealt any damage in order to wipe the stack, and then you play that card which makes all damage against a chosen target irreducible (Reveal the Flaws, I think?). Oh, Voss, do you have soak with all those minions? Well, Legacy is gonna give you one hell of a punch in the face right now ;). Even if not using it against the main villain, actually, think of something like Muninn - wouldn't need too much of a Crit Multiplier buff (if any) if combined with the make-it-irreducible thing to one-shot him and make Huginn an open target for everyone to pounce on :).

You probably need to stop looking at these decks/cards individually. Yes, some stuff is utterly useless some of the time, but other times that same useless stuff becomes absolutely epic. You don't need to hit a villain with a single hit of 20+ damage or insta-nuke all their stuff to pull off an epic result against them. There is plenty of stuff you can do and so much of it often revolves around combining effects with other decks - when some kind of random, perfect combo comes up when that hero plays that card and then you play this one, and then that other hero uses that power and KABOOM, that thing which was a serious threat last round is suddenly gone in a puff of smoke…that's the kind of stuff the game is all about. It's a team game, a co-operative game - it's not about "my deck is better/worse than your deck", it's about "hey cool, if you do that thing and I do this thing, then that really cool thing happens and we both feel really good about it". I don't think you should be thinking about the decks in isloation the way you seem to be doing - that's not what the game's about. I know you say stuff like "Oh, but the chances of that situation coming up are so low…", but well, that's half the fun - that one time you manage to pull off that epic thing out of nowhere, and it still gets mentioned months later because all the players gleefully remember how cool it was. That's why I reckon this game is so cool - it has so many possibilities, random variables and stuff that can happen as a one-off uber combo (or whatever), and you get to sit down with a bunch of people and all enjoy the uberness, and then play it again and maybe some different uberness will happen. posts.name: Edwin
posts.cooked:
Ameena:

Plinks don't do any good because it's small damage - Every little helps!

Too few little bits won't help enough.  As I've said, the game has a clock; your own HP will run out in an average of 6-9 rounds, so you're not usually able to win unless you can do it in that amount of time.  You need to aim for around 9 damage per round against Dawn, for instance; you won't do 9 in the first round, of course, you'll make up for it toward the end, but every turn in which each hero is only worth 1 or 2 damage is a round where you're not pulling adequate weight toward the goal.  This is particularly true with 3 heroes, since no villain yet created has [H]-based HP (though the Dreamer comes close, as do the Vengeance Five and the Ennead - perhaps for accuracy's sake I should say no single villain target has HP which varies this way).

~ Being irreducible doesn't matter…except when it does, like every other effect in the game. Very few abilities are useful all the time , otherwise what would be the point in having different abilities/decks/scenarios?~

Except against Miss Information, Lightning Slash is pretty much always good.  So is a card that draws you cards (and yes, Recompile does that, but not without cost).  Again, my tolerance for highly specialized weapons is greater if they are tutorable singletons; if they clog up your normal draws and get in the way when you don't need them, they're just landmines in your deck that show up now and again to give you a bad game, and that's not cool.

Also, with the max discard from Recompile you get back six cards. Six! Can anyone else draw that many at once? The only person I can think of who can manage it would be Fanatic when her only available card is Prayer of Desparation.

You have to pay four cards to draw those six, so it's only a profit of two cards besides itself.  AZ, Bunker and Tempest can all match that (though only Tempest doesn't expend his Power for the turn doing so); Scholar and with a bit of jiggering Fanatic both far exceed it, though at the cost of the rest of their turn, unless they get an OOT play.

Oh, Voss, do you have soak with all those minions? Well, Legacy is gonna give you one hell of a punch in the face right now

If it's a 90-damage punch, great.  Otherwise, those villain targets you've been leaving in play will probably just overrun the earth.  Personally, I see no reason to let Voss keep his bodyguards for any length of time.

You probably need to stop looking at these decks/cards individually. Yes, some stuff is utterly useless some of the time, but other times that same useless stuff becomes absolutely epic.

And again, search cards are the way to make that a viable strategy (though even so you occasionally get boned by the random draw, having Fanatic start with Wrathful Retribution for instance).  Or even better, modular cards - ones which have a wide variety of different uses, one of which is likely to fit the situation.  As it stands, I am forced to evaluate every card according to how often it'll do useful things (alongside how cool it is, but that's a far lower-order criterion, more of a tiebreaker than an actual factor), and if that's too low compared to how often I'm going to see it in a game, that card is a bad card.  And a deck with too many bad cards is a bad deck.  Legacy is a hero with a bad deck (some good cards, yes, but not enough of them), who is not a bad hero only because he has an absurdly good Power.  Visionary is a hero with a lot of bad cards, but I'm not sure I'd say she has a bad deck, since she has several insanely good cards and has her innate Enlighten power to accelerate and filter her draws, so cards like Brain Burn and Mass Lev are a fairly manageable inconvenience (unless you have Setback's own luck on the draw, as I seem to).

In that context, Parse strikes me as an experiment in design - building a hero with a LOT of highly situational cards, and then giving her tools to sift through them in search of the ones she'll need.  It's a neat concept, but so far I haven't seen much evidence that it performs up to spec.  Again, future plays may convince me, as they largely have with Mr. Fixer, but it's not certain.

that's the kind of stuff the game is all about. It's a team game, a co-operative game - it's not about "my deck is better/worse than your deck", it's about "hey cool, if you do that thing and I do this thing, then that really cool thing happens and we both feel really good about it".

Those moments are certainly nice to have, but I'm a bread and butter kind of guy, I don't care how good the food at Le Cordon Bleu is if I can only afford to eat there once a year, because I have to survive on something else the rest of the time, and I'd rather make sure the something else is good enough for me.  So my ideal hero is one where EVERY card in his deck is good, even if none of them are great.  I think the overall closest one is Tempest; other than duplicate Limiteds, about the only card in his deck I'm not thrilled to see is Elemental Subwave Inducer, and maybe Grevious Hail Storm but even that one is at least handy.  That doesn't mean Tempest is my overall favorite hero, but he is pretty much what I'd regard as the Gold Standard of quality, or pretty close to it.  I don't expect everyone to measure up to his level, but they have to offer something else comparably desireable, such as the extreme risk/reward equation of Absolute Zero, or the control trip you can get playing Visionary.  That last might be the best bet for me to eventually appreciate Parse, but once again, I haven't seen it happen in the three games I played (perhaps because two were against the Vengeance Five, I'm definitely done with that matchup).

I know you say stuff like "Oh, but the chances of that situation coming up are so low…", but well, that's half the fun - that one time you manage to pull off that epic thing out of nowhere, and it still gets mentioned months later because all the players gleefully remember how cool it was. That's why I reckon this game is so cool - it has so many possibilities, random variables and stuff that can happen as a one-off uber combo (or whatever), and you get to sit down with a bunch of people and all enjoy the uberness, and then play it again and maybe some different uberness will happen. Or you get utterly flattened and instead can talk about "omg remember when we got wiped by X in three rounds?", and then plot revenge against them and come back and kick their arses :D.

Eh, kinda.  I do like the way SOTM really gives me a sense of alternate timelines and shifting destinies - the way targeting is based on current HP totals (other than Lowest HP, since that never changes itself) means that just deflecting a single attack can change the outcome of the game.  So that immense variety and replayability is a definite strength - but it doesn't stop me from feeling cruddy when I draw yet another opening hand along the lines of 2x Brain Burn, 1x Mass Levitation and 1x Mind Spike.  Above all, I always live in the present moment, and so what I want is always a hero who is confident that he has the card he needs RIGHT NOW, just at his fingertips.  CR is perfect for this, Ra is pretty good, the Wraith is almost too good - there are a lot of heroes which can do this.  If Parse can't, she may well just not be the hero for me; I'll still play her an equal share of the time, but perhaps mostly in solo games.  (It's probably not a coincidence that the hero I enjoy most, Nightmist, has been played in real games a full fourth of the time, whereas my overall ratio of solo games to non-solos is more than 2 to 1.)

Humble-Knight:

Just out of curiosity, what are the bad cards in Legacy's deck?

Surge of Strength is extremely weak (unless you're Young Legacy of course), Danger Sense is situational and often unwelcome, I've mentioned Superhuman Durability as similarly being spotty in value, Next Evolution is only likely to be worth your Power against villains who concentrate heavily on a single damage type, Motivational Charge also costs a Power that you often can't spare, Fortitude is nice but seldom nice sufficient, and even Bolster Allies isn't always the best investment of your play phase.  Were I re-designing Legacy, I'd do things like making Fortitude not limited, combining DS and SHD into a single situational-defenses card, combining NE and SoS into a single card that benefits you whether you're playing offensively or defensively (but not if you're just being a cheerleader), increase the Legacy Rings to x4 in the deck, and maybe let Bolster Allies give you an extra Power usage that turn, just to make it different from Fleet of Foot.  I wouldn't mess with Inspiring Presence at all, but I might increase the self-damage on Take Down and perhaps Heroic Interception, as they're a little too good.  Maybe I'd reword Galvanize to last through your next Play phase so it could affect your One-Shots (but also your self-damages).  Lead from the Front I'd probably leave alone, it's one of those cards that's almost too good and can really shut down games in a kind of lame way, but it's so defining to what the character is all about, I'd kinda hate to mess with it.  I think that's basically his whole deck aside from the damaging one-shots.  The result of all this tweaking might actually be fun for me to play, might be brokenly overpowered, but certainly would leave me with fewer things to complain about.
